Text: {{c1::Emotional intelligence::trait}} is the ability to {{c2::identify, understand, and manage one's own emotions and the emotions of others}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: people with high emotional intelligence are the kind, caring, exceptional listeners you know.

Why: as an EMT it lets you read a scene, empathize, and stay in control when emotions run high.

Text:
Emotional intelligence is commonly understood to have five attributes:
{{c1::Self-awareness}} (recognize your own emotions)
{{c1::Self-regulation}} (control impulsive emotions and behaviors)
{{c1::Motivation}} (drive yourself and others in a positive direction)
{{c1::Empathy}} (understand others' concerns, emotions, and needs)
{{c1::Social skills}} (build and keep positive rapport and relationships)
Back Extra:
Distinguish: self-awareness is noticing your own emotions; self-regulation is controlling them.

Cue: empathy reads other people's cues; social skills act on them to build rapport.

Text:
The behavioral change stairway model is a five-step method for de-escalating a high-emotion crisis, followed in order:

1. {{c1::Employ active listening}}
2. {{c1::Display empathy}}
3. {{c1::Build a rapport}}
4. {{c1::Exert influence}}
5. {{c1::Initiate behavior change}}
Back Extra:
Cue: developed by the FBI to manage hostage negotiations; it adapts to most crisis communications.

Why: the order matters because each step builds on the ones before it to improve communication, build rapport, and de-escalate.

Text: At a scene, when a family member is not helping your patient care, a good move is to give him or her a {{c1::task to do::what}}, such as gathering medications or clothing.
Back Extra:
Why: a task turns that person from a hindrance into a valuable aide.

Pitfall: it is generally best to keep families together; separating a patient from loved ones may make the patient more anxious.

Text: People call 9-1-1 because they are in crisis, so part of being a good EMT is projecting {{c1::calm and control}} into a chaotic environment, even when you do not actually feel calm.
Back Extra:
Cue: the adage is "never let them see you sweat."

Pitfall: everything you do communicates something, so your body language must reflect your words.

Text: To help a hard-of-hearing patient hear you, have the patient put the {{c1::stethoscope}} in his or her ears while you speak softly into the {{c1::diaphragm}} to amplify the sound.
Back Extra:
Why: the stethoscope acts like a makeshift hearing aid, channeling and amplifying your voice into the patient's ears.

Cue: if you cannot communicate with the patient yourself, first have your partner try.
